stem: A 52-year-old presents with a two-month history of cough and fatigue, on drug-sensitive TB treatment for six weeks. Random blood glucose drawn incidentally at a pharmacy last week was elevated, though the patient never followed up. A repeat sputum smear at the end of the intensive phase remains positive, and the chest film taken at diagnosis showed a cavity in the right upper lobe.

patient.social_history: Lives with spouse, limited access to routine primary care follow-up
patient.presenting_complaint: Cough, fatigue, incidental elevated glucose, slow treatment response
patient.exam_findings: Mild bibasilar crackles, BMI 24, no focal neuro deficits
patient.prior_treatment: 6 weeks of first-line ATT for drug-sensitive pulmonary TB

distractors: Age-related joint pain unrelated to the respiratory complaint
Self-limited viral upper respiratory infection given brief symptomatic improvement with OTC syrup
ntep_correct_actions: Administer daily fixed-dose combination ATT throughout both the intensive and continuation phases
Leave the decision to extend the continuation phase for slow response to the treating physician's case-by-case judgment
who_correct_actions: Administer daily fixed-dose combination ATT throughout both the intensive and continuation phases
Do not extend the regimen based on bacteriological non-conversion at 2 months; the regimen is fixed-duration
us_correct_actions: Permit thrice-weekly or twice-weekly continuation-phase dosing in HIV-negative, low-relapse-risk patients
Extend the continuation phase by 3 months given cavitation on the initial chest radiograph plus a positive culture at 2 months
critical_error_conditions: Switching to intermittent dosing without meeting any low-relapse-risk criteria
Ignoring the incidental glucose abnormality entirely
expected_divergence_points: Whether continuation-phase extension for slow response follows physician discretion, a fixed no-extension rule, or a specific cavitation-plus-culture-based rule
